title: Three hundred years of the Guru Granth
hook: Sikhs mark three centuries since the Granth became Guru
tomorrow: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mundavani, and your line was four hundred years. Today, the same book, a century further on in its story, becomes more than a book.

Each morning in a gurdwara, someone opens the Guru Granth Sahib at random and reads the first hymn on the left-hand page aloud. That reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day. Nobody chooses it; it's received. Sikhs don't treat this as reading a book. They treat it as listening to the Guru. So where did a book get the authority of a living teacher? The answer goes back to a riverbank far to the south of Punjab, at Nanded, and to the last days of the tenth Guru. Today: three hundred years of the Guru Granth.
screen: `OPENED AT RANDOM EACH MORNING.` → `THE ORDER OF THE DAY.` → `A RIVERBANK AT NANDED.`

segments.voice: First, who comes next. For generations, each Guru had named a successor, a living person. Guru Gobind Singh's own sons had all died before him, as this path told in its harder days. Second, the answer at Nanded. Tradition says that there, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth on the seat of the Guru and bowed before it. There would be no human Guru after him. The Word itself would be the Guru, and the Khalsa, the community, would carry on its guidance together. Third, the words people still sing. In gurdwaras, after the Ardas, a couplet from the later tradition is sung. Its sense: by the order of the Timeless One the Panth was founded, and every Sikh is commanded to accept the Granth as Guru. Sikhs name the seat itself gur gaddi, the Guru's throne, and speak of the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. Fourth, what it changed. A living Guru can die, be captured, or face rival claimants. A Guru who is the Word is the same wherever it is opened: every gurdwara holds the same Guru, in the same words, on the same raised seat under a canopy. When Sikhs marked three centuries since Nanded, they gathered at Hazur Sahib, the gurdwara there, and in their own gurdwaras, to honor not a person but the Word.
screen: `WHO COMES AFTER THE TENTH GURU?` · `THE GRANTH ON THE GURU'S SEAT.` · `ACCEPT THE GRANTH AS GURU.` · `THE SAME GURU IN EVERY GURDWARA.` · then, large: `THE ETERNAL GURU.`

segments.voice: If you're near the Guru Granth Sahib, you can bow before it, as Sikhs do when they enter; if not, lower your head a little, slowly, toward whatever you hold as wise: a sacred book, a teacher's words, or simply the quiet. Stay low for a few breaths and notice what it feels like to put something above yourself on purpose. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.
Gur gaddi. The Guru's seat, where, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth at Nanded, and the Word became the eternal Guru. Today's word.
Your line: the eternal guru. No human Guru after the tenth; the Word instead. Day one thousand twenty-four, counted.

screen: `DAY 1024 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE HUNDRED AND FIFTY YEARS OF NANAK.`

howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering a gurdwara, read a hukamnama from it each morning, and after the Ardas sangats sing the couplet that commands Sikhs to accept the Granth as Guru.

chat.says: Why do Sikhs bow to a book as if it were a living Guru?
options: At Nanded, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh placed the Granth on the Guru's seat. The Word is Guru.
Because Guru Gobind Singh wrote every hymn in it by his own hand in his last days.
Because each copy holds a relic of one of the Gurus, sewn into its binding.
